standard.title: Text stages and language features
standard.description: identify how texts across the curriculum have different language features and are typically organised into characteristic stages depending on purposes
standard.prior_knowledge: Students describe how language features and structures in curriculum texts vary according to purpose (AC9E3LA03). They have not yet identified the characteristic stages of specific text types and how stage organisation serves social purposes.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students can identify the characteristic stages and language features of a range of curriculum text types — including narratives, information reports, explanations and arguments — and explain how stage organisation and language features together serve each text's social purpose.

nodes.label: Stages and purpose
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain that texts are organised into stages and that stages serve the text's social purpose.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify the stages of one familiar text type (e.g. narrative: orientation, complication, resolution) and explain what each stage does for the reader.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and label the stages of at least three text types from different curriculum areas — such as a narrative, an information report and an explanation — and explain the purpose each stage serves.
wider: Compare how the same social purpose (e.g. persuading) is achieved through different stage structures in different text types — argument vs advertisement vs speech
Examine how digital text forms (e.g. blog posts, infographics) adapt or modify traditional stage structures
nodes.hinge_reason: Identifying language features by text type in N2 requires students to understand what each stage is trying to do — students who conflate stages with paragraphs cannot explain why specific language features serve the stage's function.

response_modes.reason: Students often think 'stages' means paragraphs. Encountering multiple text types with labelled stages helps shift understanding from structural to functional — each stage exists because the text needs to do something at that point.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The range of curriculum text types with distinct stage structures is genuinely wide. Wider engagement builds transferable schema-awareness across subject areas.
success_criteria: Can identify the stages of a given text type and name what each stage does
Does not confuse stage with paragraph — can explain that a stage may span multiple paragraphs

nodes.label: Language features by text type
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify specific language features associated with particular text types and explain how these features serve the text's purpose.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two language features in a provided text and explain why those features suit that text type (e.g. action verbs in a recount, timeless present tense in a report).
nodes.typical_width: Identify language features across a range of text types — including verb choices, tense, noun group structure, connectives — and explain how each feature contributes to the text's purpose and stage structure.
wider: Compare language features across texts on the same topic but in different text types (e.g. an explanation and a report about the water cycle)
Examine how multimodal texts combine language features with visual features to serve the text's purpose
nodes.hinge_reason: Distinguishing explanation from report structure in N3 requires students to recognise their different language features — without the feature repertoire from N2, students can only compare surface structure, not the linguistic choices that produce it.

response_modes.reason: Language features vary across text types — students need to accumulate examples across multiple types before the distinctions between them stabilise and become reliably distinguishable.

success_criteria: Can name a language feature in a text and connect it to what the text is trying to do at that point
Can identify at least two different language features, not just one repeated example

nodes.label: Explanations and reports — structural differences
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can distinguish sequential and causal explanations from comparative and part-whole information reports by their stages and language features.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify whether a given text is an explanation or an information report and name one structural feature that supports the identification.
nodes.typical_width: Compare sequential/causal explanation structures with comparative/part-whole report structures across two or more texts, identifying the stages and language features that distinguish them.
wider: Locate examples of sequential, causal and comparative structures in texts from different curriculum areas (science, HASS, maths) and explain how the structure suits the subject content
Create a short explanation and a short report on the same topic and compare the structural choices made

response_modes.reason: Distinguishing explanation from report structure requires explicit attention to the logic of each — cause-effect chains vs classification-description hierarchies. A reasoning scaffold helps students see why the structures differ, not just that they do.

success_criteria: Can identify whether a text explains a process or reports information, and name a structural feature supporting that identification
Does not confuse sequential explanation (how something happens) with information report (what something is)

nodes.label: Form vs stage organisation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can distinguish between a text's form (poster, email, list) and its stage organisation, explaining that different forms can realise the same stages.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain the difference between a text's form and its stage organisation using one example (e.g. a poster that realises an argument has a form of 'poster' but stages of 'position, argument, conclusion').
nodes.typical_width: Identify the form and stage organisation of several texts, including cases where the same social purpose appears in different forms, and explain why form and stage organisation are separate considerations.
wider: Investigate how digital forms (social media posts, websites, infographics) organise stages differently from print equivalents while serving the same social purpose
Compare how First Nations Australian authors use different forms to structure storytelling, and consider how traditional narrative stages operate across oral and written forms
success_criteria: Can name a text's form and separately identify its stage structure
Understands that the same form (e.g. email) can realise different text types with different stage organisations
